newsitem.title: JAPAN: N.Korea says grain stocks only half what needed.
newsitem.headline: N.Korea says grain stocks only half what needed.

text.p: North Korea said on Monday it had only half the grain needed to feed its people, an announcement that appeared aimed at putting pressure on the United States to give more aid.

In an unusually frank and detailed description of the country's economic plight after two years of floods, the official Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) said North Korea's 24 million people were suffering "temporary food problems".

"As is known to all, North Korea has in recent years been repeatedly hit by unprecedented natural disasters, which greatly damaged agriculture and other sectors of the national economy and caused temporary food problems," KCNA said.

"The nation's annual demand for grain is about 7.84 million tons, of which 4.82 million tons is needed as food," it quoted a statement from a spokesman for the Flood Damage Measures Committee as saying.
"Last year's flood damage made the grain output drop to 2,502,000 tons in unhulled state, the amount being far less than expected," it said.
The KCNA report was monitored in Tokyo.

It followed a statement last week by the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies that food rations in North Korea had dropped to a level four times lower than normally considered essential for a healthy population.
The KCNA report thanked the international community for food assistance, and sought continued help.
"We are really grateful for this," KCNA said.

The Stalinist state, which in the past month has twice put off attending a U.S. briefing on proposed Korean peninsula peace talks pending a grain deal with the United States, said U.S. aid would help improve ties between the two states.

"The U.S. administration recently announced that it would continue to take part in food assistance through international agencies and encourage humanitarian assistance on the part of non-governmental organisations in the U.S.," KCNA said.
"This is noteworthy in that it is a positive move motivated by a desire for improved ties between North Korea and the U.S."

In January, Washington gave permission to Minneapolis-based Cargill Inc., the world's largest private grain trading company, to export 500,000 tonnes of wheat and/or rice to North Korea in what was expected to be a barter arrangement.
U.S. officials have told Reuters that North Korea has not made a direct link between successful completion of the Cargill deal and Pyongyang's participation at the peace talks briefing.
But they said North Korea may have thought it could get Washington to pick up some of the costs.
Tokyo-based North Korean analyst Noriyuki Suzuki of Radiopress said the KCNA report appeared to have the Cargill deal clearly in mind.
"It's a pretty blunt appeal, like, 'if you're not going to help me now I don't know what's going to happen'," Suzuki said.
"The favourable tone in describing the U.S. is also a very obvious signal urging a swift completion of negotiations with Cargill," he told Reuters.
The KCNA report took a swipe at what it said were efforts by its bitter rival South Korea to obstruct international help.

"South Korea's 'National Unification Board' recently spread groundless rumours that North Korea produced 3,690,000 tons of grain last year, or 6.9 percent higher than the previous year," the report said.
KCNA said South Korea wanted "to spoil the atmosphere of international food supply".
